Text:
‎{{c1::باب}}

Transliteration: {{c1::baab}}

{{c2::door}} — the first word she had you spell out letter by letter
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — baab

Why: baa + alif + baa. The first baa carries a vowel (the alif), the second does not — and because alif never connects to its left, the final baa stands in its independent form. She built it on the board exactly this way on 1 Sep.

Ex: it came back as word 5 of the Unit 2 dictation Drill 2 she did on the board — "baab. That's the door."

Text:
‎{{c1::اِسم}}

Transliteration: {{c1::ism}}

{{c2::name}} — the bare noun, before any "my" / "your" ending is attached
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — ism

Distinguish: ism is "a name"; add the -i ending and it becomes ismi, "my name". Dr. Khouri: "If you say ismi, that's my name. If you say ism, that's a name."

Why: possessive pronouns in Arabic are suffixes — they hang on the END of the noun.

Text:
‎{{c1::أهلاً بكَ / أهلاً بكِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::ahlan bika / ahlan biki}}

{{c2::(reply to) ahlan wa sahlan}} — to a man / to a woman
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — ahlan bika / ahlan biki

Why: bi- is a preposition like fii, and -ka / -ki is "you" — literally "welcome in you". Dr. Khouri: "We don't say that in English, but in Arabic this is what we mean."

Distinguish: Levantine swaps the preposition — ahlan fiik / ahlan fiiki.

Ex: you asked whether you can just say ahlan back — "You can say ahlan, but this is another way." And it is safe upward: "not very casual, this is neutral — older people, professors, your future boss."

Text:
‎{{c1::حَضرَتُكَ / حَضرَتُكِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::HaDratuka / HaDratuki}}

{{c2::you (polite, formal)}} — to a man / to a woman — strangers, your boss, older people
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — HaDratuka / HaDratuki

Why: HaDra is "presence", so it is literally "your presence". The -uka / -uki ending is the "you".

Ex: Dr. Khouri: "It's not just you, but a formal you. We use it with strangers, people we meet for the first time, with the boss, older people, to show extra respect." Egyptians use it a lot — "they use a lot of titles."

Distinguish: Levantine HaDartak / HaDartik — same word, the vowels shift. "If Shami is harder, use FuSHa. If FuSHa is harder, use Shami."

Pitfall: she said this one WILL be on the final — "if I bring HaDratuka on the exam, you should know what it is and how it is written."

Pitfall: capital H = Haa, the throat sound ("not from my chest, from my throat"); capital D = Daad, the emphatic d.

Text:
‎{{c1::أَنتَ / أَنتِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::anta / anti}}

{{c2::you}} — the everyday form: to a man / to a woman
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — anta / anti

Distinguish: ana = I, anta = you — she drilled them as a pair: "ana, anta."

Distinguish: Levantine inte / inti — "the a sound, most of the time, turns into e in Shami."

Distinguish: the final vowel is the whole gender — -a to a man, -i to a woman. Same pattern as -ka / -ki.

Text:
‎{{c1::اِسمُكَ / اِسمُكِ}}

Transliteration: {{c1::ismuka / ismuki}}

{{c2::your name}} — to a man / to a woman — the "your" is a suffix on the noun
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — ismuka / ismuki

Why: possessive pronouns are suffixes — -i = my (ismi), -ka = your (m), -ki = your (f). The u in the middle is a vowel on the last letter of ism, so the pieces are ism + u + ka.

Distinguish: Levantine ismak / ismik — "the suffix that indicates you-masculine is -ka or -ak."

Text:
‎{{c1::هَل}}

Transliteration: {{c1::hal}}

{{c2::the word that opens a yes/no question}} — "___ anta min madiinat Lynchburg?" = "Are you from the city of Lynchburg?"
Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — hal

Why: Arabic has no "are / is / do" at the front of a question, so hal does that job. Dr. Khouri: "Anytime you want to ask 'are you, is he, is she, are we', in Arabic we add hal."

Distinguish: hal opens a yes/no question · maa opens a "what" question · ayna opens a "where" question.

Pitfall: NOT in the Alif Baa Unit 2 list — she put it on the slide on 1 Sep, the way she added askun last week. No book audio exists for it.

Ex: hal anta min madiinat Lynchburg? — answer nacam or laa.
